title: Netflix Turns Operational Data Into a Knowledge Graph for AI-Driven Observability
gist: Netflix is building an ontology-driven knowledge graph (Observability Ontology on RDF/OWL/SHACL/SPARQL, stored in its Rust-based QuipuDB) that links apps, incidents, deployments, alerts and dependencies so engineers and AI agents can cut ~4-hour regression investigations. The graph, populated by deterministic and LLM-based enrichers, underpins AutoRCA, its agentic root-cause system, with the long-term aim of automated remediation and self-healing infrastructure under human approval.

insights.claim: Netflix says it handles more than 2 billion requests daily and upwards of 38 million real-time logging events every second, and supported about 65 million concurrent streams during the November 2024 Jake Paul-Mike Tyson fight.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Quantifies the operational scale that makes manual incident investigation untenable.
insights.locator: The company claims it handles more than 2 billion

insights.claim: At Netflix, investigating a typical application regression can take around four hours, with much of that time spent reconstructing relationships between systems rather than analysing the underlying data.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Points to relationship context, not more telemetry, as the main lever for cutting incident costs.
insights.quote: much of that time spent reconstructing relationships between systems rather than analysing the underlying data
insights.locator: The company claims it handles more than 2 billion

insights.claim: Netflix's metrics, events, logs, and traces (MELT) are scattered across alerting, incident management, deployment tooling, and engineering communication platforms, forcing engineers to manually connect evidence for regressions that may stem from client releases, experiments, load shedding, or distant downstream services.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Fragmented tooling is the problem semantic-layer observability vendors aim to solve.
insights.locator: Netflix already collects metrics, events, logs

insights.claim: Netflix concluded the missing capability was a consistent way to describe not just individual operational components but how they relate, and built an Observability Ontology defining entities, properties, and relationships.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Semantic models are emerging as foundational infrastructure for AI-driven operations.

insights.claim: Netflix's ontology uses established semantic-web standards RDF, OWL, SHACL, and SPARQL, and the knowledge graph is stored in QuipuDB, Netflix's distributed RDF database built on Rust's redb storage engine.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Large-scale adoption could revive interest in graph/RDF databases as an AI-ops data layer.
insights.locator: Its Observability Ontology provides that common model

insights.claim: Netflix populates the graph through enrichers that turn operational system data into subject-predicate-object triples, mixing deterministic stages with LLM and probabilistic stages constrained by strict validation such as consistent entity types, URI naming conventions, and checks against its software catalogue.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Shows a pattern for safely using LLMs in data pipelines: probabilistic extraction gated by deterministic validation.

insights.claim: Netflix captures incident-discussion content, including hypotheses, rejected explanations, and mitigation decisions, so human reasoning becomes part of the operational knowledge base instead of disappearing when the conversation ends.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Institutional incident knowledge becomes a compounding data asset for AI agents.
insights.locator: Netflix also captures information from incident

insights.claim: Netflix's correlation engine examines 13 signal types, including log errors, metric anomalies, traces, alerts, incidents, deployments, configuration changes, experiments, and code changes, weighing evidence like temporal proximity and severity to produce ranked causal hypotheses.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Ranked, evidence-backed hypotheses are the product target for AIOps tools.

insights.claim: Netflix frames its approach as a knowledge flywheel of Observe, Enrich, Infer, and Adapt, where insights from investigations feed future detection and analysis.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Compounding-data flywheels give in-house platforms at scale an advantage over generic tooling.
insights.locator: Netflix describes the process as a knowledge flywheel

insights.claim: The knowledge graph underpins AutoRCA, Netflix's internal agentic AI system for root-cause analysis, where specialist agents for traces, logs, or deployments use the ontology as a common interface instead of exchanging loosely structured findings.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: A shared ontology as the multi-agent interface is a design pattern that may generalize across enterprise agent systems.
insights.quote: they use the ontology as a common interface
insights.locator: Rather than having specialist agents exchange

themes.theme: Path to self-healing and competitive context

insights.claim: Netflix intends to produce ranked, evidence-backed incident explanations while humans retain approval authority over proposed changes and remediation.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Human-in-the-loop remains the governance norm for AI ops even at leading-edge adopters.
insights.locator: Netflix intends to use this foundation

insights.claim: Netflix ultimately wants to extend automated root-cause analysis into automated remediation and self-healing infrastructure, and plans to explore integration with its Unified Data Architecture to connect operational data with broader business and technology domains.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Signals the direction of travel for AIOps: from diagnosis to autonomous remediation.
insights.locator: The company ultimately wants to extend

insights.claim: While Datadog, Dynatrace, and Splunk already correlate observability signals and increasingly add AI to incident investigation, Netflix's approach differs by emphasizing a persistent semantic model of operational relationships accessible to engineers and machines.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Pressure on observability vendors (DDOG, DT) to offer semantic/knowledge-graph layers, or risk large customers building in-house.
insights.locator: Platforms such as Datadog, Dynatrace, and Splunk
